Introduction

A stroke can happen suddenly, without warning, and every minute can matter. When blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a blood vessel ruptures, brain cells can begin to become damaged.

Recognizing the warning signs quickly is therefore critical. Knowing how to identify sudden facial drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulties, vision or balance changes, and other possible symptoms can help someone seek emergency medical care without delay.

The B.E. F.A.S.T. approach provides a simple way to remember some of the most important warning signs of stroke. Understanding these signs—and knowing what to do when they appear—can potentially make a life-changing difference.

What Is a Stroke?

A stroke is a medical emergency that occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is interrupted or when a blood vessel in or around the brain ruptures and causes bleeding.

There are two major types of stroke:

* Ischemic stroke: occurs when a blood vessel supplying the brain becomes blocked, usually by a blood clot or other obstruction.
* Hemorrhagic stroke: occurs when a blood vessel ruptures, causing bleeding within the brain or in the surrounding spaces.

In either situation, brain tissue can become damaged because normal blood supply and oxygen delivery are disrupted.

Recognizing the Warning Signs

Stroke symptoms often develop suddenly. They may include:

* Sudden difficulty walking or loss of balance
* Sudden vision changes
* Facial drooping, particularly on one side
* Sudden weakness or numbness, especially affecting one side of the body
* Difficulty speaking or understanding speech
* A sudden, severe headache with no known cause, particularly in some hemorrhagic strokes

The American Stroke Association recommends the B.E. F.A.S.T. approach for recognizing common stroke warning signs:

B – Balance: Sudden loss of balance or coordination
E – Eyes: Sudden vision changes
F – Face: Facial drooping or an uneven smile
A – Arm: Sudden arm weakness or numbness
S – Speech: Slurred speech or difficulty speaking or understanding
T – Time: Time to seek emergency medical care

Recognizing these signs quickly can make a critical difference.

Why Is Time So Important?

Stroke treatment is highly time-sensitive because prolonged interruption of blood flow can result in progressive brain injury.

For appropriately selected patients with acute ischemic stroke, current AHA/ASA guidance supports intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of symptom onset or last known well in eligible patients.

Importantly, treatment is not necessarily limited to this conventional time window. Selected patients may qualify for thrombolysis beyond 4.5 hours when advanced brain imaging demonstrates characteristics suggesting that potentially salvageable brain tissue remains.

Similarly, endovascular thrombectomy is an established treatment for eligible patients with certain large-vessel occlusion strokes. In appropriately selected patients, treatment can be beneficial well beyond the earliest hours after symptom onset.

Therefore, the absence of treatment within the first few hours should not be interpreted as a reason to give up or delay emergency evaluation.

What Should You Do If Stroke Symptoms Occur?

If someone suddenly develops symptoms suggestive of stroke:

Do not wait for the symptoms to improve.

Do not simply put the person to sleep or “sleep it off.”

Do not self-medicate.

Seek emergency medical care immediately and note the exact time the symptoms first appeared, or the last time the person was known to be well.

This information can be extremely important when doctors determine which treatments may be appropriate.

What If the Symptoms Disappear?

Even if the symptoms completely disappear, urgent medical evaluation is still necessary.

Temporary neurological symptoms may represent a transient ischemic attack (TIA), which can be a warning sign of an impending major stroke.

A person who appears completely normal again may still require urgent assessment to identify the underlying cause and reduce the risk of a subsequent stroke.

Time Is Brain

Stroke is one of the clearest examples of why recognizing an emergency and acting quickly matters.

Knowing the warning signs, remembering B.E. F.A.S.T., recording the time symptoms began, and seeking emergency medical care immediately can help patients reach potentially time-sensitive treatment sooner.

Recognize the signs. Act immediately. Time is Brain.
